newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya reform leaders wary of KANU proposals.
newsitem.headline: Kenya reform leaders wary of KANU proposals.

text.p: Leaders of a political reform campaign in Kenya were unconvinced on Friday by ruling party moves to meet their demands and said they would stick to their crusade for change.

The ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party announced on Thursday constitutional changes to pull the reform rug from under an opposition-backed alliance, which had forged unity among opponents of President Daniel arap Moi.
The move surprised opposition leaders and stunned ordinary Kenyans, who struggled on Friday to understand, clustering in small groups around newspapers laid out for sale on Nairobi's streets.

"It's too early for us to raise the flag and say we are all on board," opposition politician Richard Leakey told Reuters. "I think by the middle of next week we should have more evidence of what is going on."

"There is nothing I have seen so far that convinces me their commitment is genuine. We must see what is brought to parliament next week," added Leakey, the secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party and a world renowned palaeontologist.

KANU's National Executive Council chaired by Moi proposed parliament set up a commission to review Kenya's constitution and pass a bill for 11 controversial laws to be "repealed or amended where necessary" before this year's general election.
Opposition leaders said they wanted the 11 laws repealed, as the minimal reforms they demanded for free and fair elections. The constitutional review would be completed after the polls.
If enacted by parliament, where KANU has a majority, the repeal of the 11 laws would reduce the power of Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years before presidential and parliamentary polls.

"I am apprehensive. KANU is trying to stem the crisis, not to change genuinely," said Reverend Timothy Njoya, a Presbyterian cleric who like Leakey is a member of the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) behind the reform drive.
"We don't want them (KANU) to represent themselves as the reformists. But we welcome KANU's change of heart," he said.

But the confusion generated by KANU appeared to have hit at popular support for the NCEC. Minutes after the time by the reform movement set for the start of an open air prayer service in a Nairobi park on Friday, only a few people had gathered.

Njoya's arm was broken by police on July 7 during clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in Nairobi and several other cities and towns. At least nine people were killed in the worst political violence to hit in Kenya in seven years.
The July 7 clashes were followed by student unrest, prompting tourist cancellations and a crisis of confidence among investors. Tourism is Kenya's main foreign exchange earner.

KANU's proposals were announced after the NCEC called for a series of new "mass actions" including a rally in Kenya's second city Mombasa, the centre of its coast tourism industry, on July 26 and a nationwide general strike and sit-in on August 8.
Members of KANU's National Executive Council went beyond a statement issued after Thursday's meeting which made proposals and said that they were meeting opposition demands for reform.

"They asked for so-called minimum constitutional (political) reforms. We have not only agreed to these, but have also proposed that comprehensive reforms be examined," said NEC member Nicholas Biwott, a government minister of state.

Bills to be repealed or amended included the Public Order Act regulating public meetings, the Preservation of Public Security Act providing for detention without trial and the Societies Act, under which all parties must be registered.
